concepts.title: 1. Plotting (x, y) & Quadrants
concepts.subtitle: Navigating the 2D Grid
concepts.summary: Points are represented as (x, y), where x is the horizontal coordinate and y is the vertical coordinate. The two axes divide the plane into four quadrants.

points.text: Coordinate Order: Always read an ordered pair as $(x,y)$: x first, y second.
Origin: The point $(0,0)$ is where the two axes meet.
Axes: If x=0, the point lies on the y-axis; if y=0, it lies on the x-axis.

concepts.trap: Do not swap the coordinates. $(3,-2)$ is in Quadrant IV, while $(-2,3)$ is in Quadrant II.

concepts.title: 2. Reading Intercepts from Graphs
concepts.subtitle: Locating Axis Crossings
concepts.summary: An intercept is the point where a graph meets an axis. For algebraic equations, set the other coordinate to zero to find the intercept.

points.text: x-intercept: Set $y=0$ and solve for x. The point has the form $(x,0)$.
y-intercept: Set $x=0$ and solve for y. The point has the form $(0,y)$.
Quadratic Curves: The x-intercepts are the roots where the graph crosses or touches the x-axis.

concepts.trap: Always identify which coordinate is zero. For an x-intercept, y=0; for a y-intercept, x=0.

concepts.title: 3. Parallel, Intersecting & Coincident Lines
concepts.subtitle: Comparing Linear Relationships
concepts.summary: Two straight lines may meet at one point, never meet, or overlap completely. Their slopes and intercepts provide a visual and algebraic test.

points.text: Intersecting: Different slopes produce exactly one intersection point and therefore one ordered-pair solution.
Parallel: Equal slopes with different intercepts mean the lines never meet.
Coincident: Equal slopes and equal intercepts mean both equations describe the same line.

concepts.formula: m_1\neq m_2\implies\text{Intersecting},\quad m_1=m_2,\ c_1\neq c_2\implies\text{Parallel},\quad m_1=m_2,\ c_1=c_2\implies\text{Coincident}
concepts.trap: Equal slopes alone do not prove coincidence. You must also check the intercepts, or equivalently the ratio of all coefficients.

steps.hint: In slope-intercept form, y=mx+c.

steps.strategy_question: What are the y-intercepts?

option_details.explanation: The constant term c is the y-intercept in y=mx+c.
2 is the slope of each line.
The signs have been reversed.
The intercepts belong to the specific equations: 3 and -5.

steps.rubric_text: Did you distinguish slope from y-intercept?

steps.strategy_question: What does equal slope but different intercepts imply?

option_details.explanation: Equal slopes with different y-intercepts produce distinct parallel lines.
Different slopes are required for ordinary intersection at one point.
Coincident lines also require equal intercepts.
Perpendicularity requires a slope relationship such as m1m2=-1, not equal slopes.

steps.rubric_text: Did you use both equal slopes and unequal intercepts?
steps.hint: Same slope, different vertical position.

revisit_topic.tip: Parallel lines have no common point.
